newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Air raid, bomb in Kabul kill seven, wound 69.
newsitem.headline: Air raid, bomb in Kabul kill seven, wound 69.

text.p: An air raid and a bomb blast in the Afghan capital Kabul on Sunday killed at least seven people and wounded 69, government sources and a private news service said.
Kabul radio, monitored in Islamabad, said two jets of the forces commanded by northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum had carried out the raid, killing four people and wounding 32.

It also blamed "enemies of Islam", a reference to opponents of the Taleban Islamic movement that now governs most of Afghanistan, for the bomb blast in a busy central Kabul market area which a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said killed three people and wounded 37.
Forces opposing the Taleban Islamic militia which controls Kabul have launched a number of air raids on the capital since suffering a defeat on front lines north of the city a week ago.
Tens of thousands had gathered at four sites to pray for rain at the request of Taleban leader Mullah Mohammed Omar.
The bombs landed in northeast Kabul about a mile (two km) from the site of the biggest gathering.
Doctors had earlier said four people were killed and 15 wounded, including a U.N. employee, in the aid raid. But the radio put the number of injured at 32, including a child with serious wounds.
The bomb blast at Faroshgar market area "killed several people and wounded some others", the radio said.
However, the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press agency said three people were killed and 37 wounded by the blast.

Earlier, one plane swooped low over the city and dropped four bombs on the residential district of Wazir Akbar Khan, destroying three houses, including the office of the United Nations World Health Organisation.
Another bomb damaged the outer wall of the United States Embassy, unused since 1989.
The Taleban captured Kabul in September from the ousted government of president Burhanuddin Rabbani and now controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan. It is enforcing a strict Islamic code.
Shortly after the raid, anti-aircraft gunners of the ruling Taleban Islamic movement criss-crossed the sky with tracer fire but did not appear to have hit any plane.
Taleban fighters commandeered cars to take the wounded to hospital in the absence of the city's ambulance service, a victim of five years of internecine warfare in the capital.
Frightened residents huddled in the gateways of their burnt-out houses as Taleban fighters searched for dead and wounded among the rubble.
